title: Chess 4-Week
subtitle: Sharp tactics, checkmate patterns & calm endgames

cards.front: What are the 3 golden rules of the first 10 moves?
cards.back: 1) Claim the center (e4/d4), 2) Develop knights & bishops once toward active squares, 3) Castle early to connect rooks.
cards.example: Before pushing a flank pawn or moving the same piece twice, ask: 'Are all my minor pieces in the game and is my king safe?'

cards.front: How do you spot a Knight Fork in under 3 seconds?
cards.hint: Color geometry: knights always alternate square colors
cards.back: Two enemy pieces can only be forked by a knight if they stand on the SAME color square! Look at opposite-colored jump squares between them.
cards.example: Classic target: Black King on e8 and Rook on a8 (both dark squares) → Nc7+ (light square) wins the exchange.

cards.front: You pinned an enemy knight to their queen with Bg5. What is the master rule next?
cards.hint: Don't rush to capture — pile up!
cards.back: A pinned piece can't flee: add more attackers (especially a pawn or knight) rather than trading it off immediately.
cards.example: Absolute pin (to the King) = illegal to move. Relative pin (to the Queen) = legal, so always watch for desperado checks!

cards.front: What is the CCT checklist before every single move?
cards.hint: Calculate the most forcing moves first — for BOTH sides
cards.back: Checks → Captures → Threats. Scan all three for yourself, then scan your opponent's CCT replies before lifting a piece.
cards.example: 90% of club blunders vanish the moment CCT becomes an automatic 5-second breath before moving.

cards.front: What makes a Discovered Check the deadliest tactic on the board?
cards.hint: The moving piece gets a 'free turn'
cards.back: Because the opponent MUST answer the uncovered check, your stepping piece can capture an undefended piece—even while standing en prise.
cards.example: Double check is even stronger: neither blocking nor capturing works; the enemy king is forced to move.

cards.front: An enemy knight on f6 is the sole defender of both h7 (mate) and d5. What motif strikes?
cards.back: Capture or sacrifice against one duty (e.g., Bxf6 or Nxd5) so the overloaded defender drops the other critical square.
cards.example: Whenever one piece guards two vital squares, treat it as uninsured.

cards.front: Smothered Mate: Queen on b3, Knight on g5, Black King castled on g8 (Rf8, pawns g7/h7). Find the finish!
cards.hint: Kh8 → Nf7+ → Kg8 → Nh6++ → Kh8 → Qg8+!
cards.back: 1. Nf7+ Kg8 2. Nh6+ Kh8 (double check!) 3. Qg8+! Rxg8 4. Nf7# — Philidor's Legacy.
cards.example: Rxg8 is forced because the knight covers f7, sealing Black's own king inside a cage.

cards.front: What is a 'Knight Outpost', and what makes it permanent?
cards.back: A square in enemy territory anchored by your pawn that NO enemy pawn can ever attack (typically in front of a backward pawn).
cards.example: A knight firmly planted on the 6th rank is often worth as much as a rook.

cards.front: Why are doubled rooks on the 7th rank called 'Pigs on the 7th'?
cards.hint: Unmoved enemy pawns + trapped enemy king
cards.back: They devour base pawns laterally while trapping the opposing king on the back rank, setting up unstoppable mating nets or perpetuals.
cards.example: Step 1: Seize the open file. Step 2: Double rooks. Step 3: Penetrate to the 7th rank.

cards.front: What is Direct Opposition in King + Pawn vs. King endgames?
cards.hint: One empty square directly between the two kings, NOT your turn
cards.back: Kings face each other with one square between them; the side NOT to move holds the opposition, forcing the other king to yield ground.
cards.example: Key rule: get your KING in front of your pawn first (e.g., pawn e4, King e6) to escort promotion.

cards.front: Can the defending king catch a runaway passed pawn without counting move by move?
cards.hint: Draw a diagonal from the pawn to the promotion rank
cards.back: Visualize a square from the pawn to the 8th rank. If the enemy king stands inside—or can step inside on its move—it catches the pawn.
cards.example: Watch out: a pawn on its starting 2nd rank shrinks the square by one rank thanks to its double-step!

cards.front: Lucena vs. Philidor: the single most important principle of all rook endgames?
cards.hint: Where does a rook belong relative to a passed pawn?
cards.back: Rooks belong BEHIND passed pawns—both your own and your opponent's. Activity beats a passive extra pawn.
cards.example: Lucena wins by 'building a bridge' (shielding your king from checks with your rook on the 4th/5th rank).
